transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Venkataraman (CTO - LotusWare), Derek Simmons (ML Lead), Ana Ruiz (Infra)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the account lead, and with me is Liam, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in — we've been evaluating a few routes and want to map tradeoffs quickly.
[00:12] Derek: Yep, hi all. We've got a pretty specific bar for latency and multilingual fidelity, so hoping to get into the weeds.
[00:19] Liam: Great. Quick agenda: we want to understand your workloads (context lengths, languages, tools), then talk model options and hosting modes, and finish with next steps. Sound ok?
[00:27] Priya: Yep. To start, our product is a support automation layer for SMB merchants. Typical request is a conversation history plus product catalog context — sometimes up to ~20k tokens when threads are long, but mostly 2–6k. We also need Spanish and Hindi support for a small but growing segment.
[00:45] Maya: That's helpful. Two quick clarifying q's: 1) do you need synchronous sub-second responses for UI flows, or is 1–2s acceptable? 2) what's your annual request volume estimate?
[00:54] Derek: For chat UI, 1–1.5s for top-level completions is ideal. For background tasks (summaries, batching), 2–4s is fine. Request volume — current production is ~40k queries/month, 6 months projection 200k/mo.
[01:10] Ana: On infra constraints: some customers require data to remain in our VPC on prem racks; we have an internal compliance committee that will push back on hosted unless proper audit controls are in place.
[01:20] Maya: Understood — so Private or Dedicated might be relevant. We'll walk the differences.
[01:23] Liam: Quick framing: Hosted = fastest onboarding, usage-based, Redwood-managed infra; Dedicated = reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation; Private = control plane in your VPC or on-prem for strict data residency and network isolation. Each has different latency and ops tradeoffs.
[01:39] Priya: For us the big question is cost vs latency and the complexity of running on-prem. We're leaning away from fully managing everything but can't do hosted unless we hit certain audit criteria.
[01:49] Derek: Also model selection — we've run prototypes with OpenAI (gpt-4o) and a couple of open models via Hugging Face. Topline: OpenAI high quality but costy; open models cheaper but we saw hallucination on product-specific queries and Spanish sometimes worse.
[02:05] Liam: Totally expected. For open models, pick is often between Llama/Llama3-family, Mistral, and some of the newer Mosaic/Code models depending on task. Important: quantization and KV cache behavior changes per model — that affects latency for long contexts.
[02:23] Priya: Can you explain KV cache again? Our infra folks mentioned it but it's fuzzy.
[02:28] Liam: Sure — KV cache means the key-value attention cache saved for the conversation so subsequent tokens don't re-compute full attention for the prefix. For long histories, a model runtime that manages KV cache efficiently reduces cost per token and improves throughput. But some quantized runtimes or model conversions can break streaming or make cache restoration slow.
[02:46] Derek: So for 20k token threads — what do you recommend? A long-context model or retrieved-context approach?
[02:52] Maya: Probably a mix. For strictly conversational continuity you want a model with native long context (32k) or chunking with retrieval for older turns. Redwood supports model routing and prefix caching to make that hybrid flow cheaper.
[03:06] Priya: On multilingual: Spanish was a problem with the open models we tried. Is there a list of models you recommend for en/es/hi?
[03:14] Liam: Yes — for high quality across en/es/hi, larger Llama3 variants and some Mistral-large fine-tuned families are competitive. There are also community forks that boost multilingual, but you trade support and certainties. We can share a curated model matrix.
[03:25] Derek: Are those available in Hosted? And how do you handle model variants for Dedicated/Private?
[03:30] Maya: Hosted has a model catalog with Redwood-verified performance profiles. For Dedicated you can reserve the same model variants (we deploy to your capacity). Private supports bringing your own model bundles — we assist with onboarding and kernel selection.
[03:42] Ana: On Private, is there an on-prem installer or is it a VPC package? We have air-gapped sites.
[03:47] Liam: We support both: private control plane with VPC connectors and a separate on-prem package for air-gapped deployments. For air-gapped, you'll run Redwood runtime with our ops tooling; there are additional prerequisites (KMS gateway for key exchanges or HSM integration). We have a playbook.
[04:04] Priya: Ok. Let's talk about latencies — you mentioned kernel selection. How much tuning is needed to hit 1–1.5s for short chats?
[04:13] Liam: It depends on model size and hardware. For a 7–13B model on A10/NVIDIA 40-class hardware, 1–1.5s for short completions is realistic with continuous batching and optimized kernels. For 70B+ models you'll need multi-GPU setup — latency rises unless you do sharding + micro-batching. Dedicated lets you size for that predictability.
[04:34] Derek: So from a cost perspective, probably 13B or 33B family on Dedicated might be our sweet spot. But Spanish/Hindi quality — do we need an instruction-finetuned variant?
[04:44] Liam: Instruction fine-tuning helps. Another approach: use a smaller multilingual base and add an adapter or lightweight fine-tune on your domain prompts. That reduces footprint and often improves hallucinations on product data.
[04:57] Priya: Tool-calling — we need the model to make DB lookups and call a product-retrieval tool (we have an internal API). What's the pattern?
[05:05] Maya: Typical pattern: you either do retrieval-first (query embedding, fetch documents, pass to model) or allow the model to call a tool (function calling style) and then execute the tool server-side. Redwood supports both: streaming function-call-like flows and structured output so you can map back to your API.
[05:20] Derek: We tried naive tool-calling and saw a lot of spurious calls — model asked to fetch everything. Is there a guardrail?
[05:27] Liam: Yes — we recommend a combination of prompt-engineered constraints, a scoring layer that validates tool call intents, and rate-limiting on tool invocation. On Dedicated/Private you can plug the validation step inside your network.
[05:38] Ana: About security: we need SSO (SAML/Okta), audit logs, and KMS for keys. Also, if we go Private, does Redwood still have any access to logs?
[05:49] Maya: For Private, you manage the control plane and logs — Redwood doesn't see customer payloads unless expressly arranged for support. We integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Dedicated, logs can be configured to forward to your SIEM; we also provide token-level cost breakdowns in the console.
[06:03] Priya: Sounds good. What about evals — we want quality metrics across en/es/hi and hallucination rate on product retrieval. Can you help run those?
[06:12] Liam: Absolutely. We can run model evals using your prompt set and dataset, produce ROUGE/bleu-like metrics where applicable, plus a hallucination scoring based on reference data. We recommend a baseline with Hosted models and then run the same tests on Dedicated/Private deployment to compare latency and cost.
[06:29] Derek: Bench details — do you need traffic replay or synthetic traffic?
[06:33] Liam: Either. Replay of real representative traffic is best — that gives us cache hit patterns and request distribution. If you can't share full data, a sampled anonymized set works. We'll sign an NDA if needed.
[06:43] Priya: One of our constraints is tokenization differences across models — that can explode cost unexpectedly. Any guidance?
[06:50] Liam: Tokenization variance is real. We include tokenization estimates in our model matrix and tooling. In practice we recommend running tokenization on a sample of your corpus to estimate unit costs per model. We also have token-counting hooks in the SDK.
[07:01] Derek: About quantization — we saw faster throughput with 4-bit but some drop in multilingual quality. Is that expected?
[07:08] Liam: Yes. Aggressive quantization helps inference speed/cost but can impact certain language nuances. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload: e.g., 4-bit for high-frequency english-only completion; 8-bit or FP16 for multilingual or retrieval-heavy flows.
[07:22] Maya: Quick pivot — competitors. Are you evaluating any other platforms beyond what you mentioned?
[07:26] Priya: We're talking to a few managed providers and also trying a homegrown cluster with Hugging Face because of cost control. The team is worried about the ops burden.
[07:36] Maya: Makes sense. Our value prop is the unified runtime + ops tooling so you don't have to reverse-engineer kernel selection and cache behavior.
[07:44] Derek: What about rollout strategies? We want canaries and A/B tests across models.
[07:49] Liam: Redwood Console supports per-route model assignments, canary rollouts, A/B testing, and automatic fallback policies if latency or quality regressions are detected. We tie quality alerts to your eval prompts so you get notified on regressions.
[08:03] Priya: Great. Cost math: can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated?
[08:08] Maya: Ballpark — hosted: pay per token, good for early trials and variable traffic. Dedicated: monthly reserved capacity yields lower per-token cost at scale and predictable latency. Private: higher upfront but required for compliance. We can provide detailed pricing bands after we know model choices and QPS.
[08:24] Derek: For our projected 200k/mo in six months, which path typically wins?
[08:29] Liam: At 200k/mo, Dedicated often becomes more economical if you need consistent latency and have sustained peak load, especially with caching. Hosted can still work if you want operational simplicity and less up-front commitment.
[08:42] Priya: Let's talk an example flow — customer asks in Spanish about order status, model needs to check product DB and return structured status plus human-friendly text. Latency target: 1.5s. How do we design that?
[08:55] Liam: Recommended: 1) pre-embed recent customer history + product metadata into a retrieval store, 2) on request, do a fast embedding lookup (50–200ms), attach top-K docs (short), then call a 13B multilingual model with streaming for final text. Tool-call should be used only when retrieval fails or an explicit action is needed. This usually fits in ~1–1.5s on Dedicated with tuned batching.
[09:18] Derek: If retrieval adds 200–300ms, plus model 600–900ms, we're borderline but seems doable.
[09:24] Liam: Yep, tuning and edge caching matter — prefix cache can cut per-token compute for repeated flows.
[09:29] Priya: Any gotchas for Spanish/Hindi with embeddings?
[09:33] Liam: Embedding quality varies — multilingual embedding models exist but you should benchmark similarity on your docs. If you have multilingual docs, a multilingual embedding model is recommended; else, translate before embedding (but that has costs).
[09:45] Priya: On dataset privacy, if we do hosted evals, will data be stored?
[09:49] Maya: Hosted defaults are configurable; for evals we can set retention windows and opt-out of training. We'll send our data handling policy.
[09:57] Derek: Great. On deployment timeline — if we pick Dedicated, how long to ramp?
[10:02] Maya: Typical Dedicated onboarding is 2–6 weeks depending on capacity and benchmarking needs; Private on-prem tends to be 4–10 weeks because of networking and HSM/KMS setup.
[10:12] Ana: For air-gapped sites, 4–10 weeks seems optimistic — we have customs and security approvals, so plan for extra time.
[10:19] Liam: Totally — we can make a phased plan: start with Hosted for evals, then move to Dedicated pilot, and Private if required.
[10:27] Priya: One operational question: if we deploy multiple model variants, can Redwood route by language or latency automatically?
[10:33] Liam: Yes — smart routing policies let you route by inferred language, latency budget, or cost tier. You can also do model A/B by route.
[10:40] Derek: Curious about model updates — say upstream model releases a new Llama3 patch, how are regressions handled?
[10:45] Maya: We support pinned model versions and canaries. We also run continuous evals against your prompt sets and alert on regressions. If a new model shows worse hallucination we won't automatically flip you over.
[10:58] Priya: Good. Pricing again — can you provide an example TCO for 200k/mo across the three modes?
[11:05] Maya: We'll produce a TCO spreadsheet but rough: Hosted might be higher per-token, let's say X; Dedicated reduces per-token by 20–50% depending on reserved slots; Private adds platform license + ops. We'll send tailored numbers.
[11:17] Derek: For benchmarks, when can we run them?
[11:20] Liam: We can schedule a bench next week if you can share a sample dataset and open a tunnnel or provide replay. Derek, you mentioned a window?
[11:27] Derek: Yes, we can give a 24–48 hour window for a replay — will coordinate.
[11:31] Ana: We'll need an internal ticket for network access and firewall rules — I'll share the contact points.
[11:36] Maya: Noted.
[11:38] Priya: Any final technical pitfalls we should watch for?
[11:41] Liam: A few: tokenization surprises, quantization quality drop for low-resource languages, and the need to validate tool-call intents. Also watch for cold-start latency on large models if your capacity is autoscaled — keep reserved slots for predictable UI latency.
[11:58] Derek: About autoscale — does Redwood offer burst capacity for Dedicated?
[12:02] Maya: Yes, you can configure burst capacity and autoscaling policies. We also offer fallback routing to smaller models if the preferred model is slow.
[12:12] Priya: That fallback sounds useful — what's the fallback behavior for stateful chats?
[12:15] Liam: Fallback returns a shorter summary or a clarified question, or routes to a smaller model that can handle the state. We recommend designing the UX to tolerate occasional fallbacks.
[12:26] Priya: Ok good.
[12:28] Maya: Let's recap next steps: Maya will send the model performance spreadsheet and pricing bands; Liam will prepare a bench plan and initial eval config; Derek will provide the sample prompt set and traffic window; Ana will confirm network/firewall windows and compliance contacts.
[12:42] Priya: That works. Anything else?
[12:45] Derek: One last thing — can Redwood share a short doc on tokenizer measurement and cost estimation?
[12:50] Liam: We'll include that in the spreadsheet.
[12:53] Priya: Great. Thanks, everyone.
[12:56] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[13:00] End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard brand names (e.g., Mistral spelled "Mistral" but model forks may be transcribed differently), some speaker overlaps during q&a.
